#7846. If You Commit a Crime with a Gun, You Might Not Want to Use a Purple Gun with a Blue Laser Sight

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

And if you do plan on doing that, you might not want to make a rap video depicting that very gun.

From Commonwealth v. Ashford, decided two weeks ago by a Pennsylvania appellate court, in an opinion by Judge Mary Murray, joined by Judges Timika Lane and Kate Ford Elliott:

The trial court summarized the evidence adduced at Appellant's jury trial …

On February 11, 2023, … [(Ms. South)] was carjacked in Reading City, Berks County, Pennsylvania, by three men in black balaclavas[, one of whom] brandish[ed a] handgun[ ] with blue laser sights….

The evening prior, on February 10, 2023, a video [("the video" or "the YouTube video")] was uploaded to the online video sharing platform[,] YouTube[,] depicting Appellant and [two] other men in black balaclavas handling and displaying various firearms with blue laser sights, including a purple Glock handgun. [The video was admitted into evidence and played for the jury at trial, albeit without sound.] The video itself is undated, though Appellant appears to be around the same age [in the video and at the time of the offense,] and is depicted wearing the same sweatshirt in which he was apprehended ten days later.

{The video, which is a part of the certified record, remains posted on YouTube. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=W-IX9rvOflg (last visited Oct. 1, 2026); N.T., 5/15/25, Commonwealth Ex. 1. At several points during the two-minute-long video, Appellant (1) partially removes his facial covering, revealing his face; and (2) is holding a purple Glock handgun equipped with a blue laser sight. The video is accompanied by background music that was created by a rap musician with whom Appellant claims to have no association.} …

Approximately ten days later, on February 20, 2023, Officer Redinger of the Northwest Regional Police identified Ms. South's stolen car while on patrol in Mount Joy Township, Lancaster County, Pennsylvania. When [Officer Redinger] attempted to pull the car over using lights and sirens, the vehicle fled. Several minutes later, law enforcement officers were eventually able to stop the fleeing vehicle using spike strips. Four male occupants, including Appellant, emerged and fled on foot in different directions[,] in pairs of two.

Sergeant [Seth] Arnold [(Sergeant Arnold)] of the Northwest Regional Police chased two of the males, including Appellant, behind a nearby residence. Sergeant Arnold was able to apprehend Appellant when [Appellant] tripped and fell near a trampoline in the backyard [of a residence].

When Sergeant Arnold retraced Appellant's path of flight, he observed a bright blue light shining in the grass near the trampoline. Closer inspection revealed the light to be emanating from a purple Glock handgun with a blue laser attachment….

Appellant contends the trial court's improper admission of the video violated his right to free expression ….

"[T]he government generally lacks the authority to restrict expression based on its message, topic, ideas, or content." Our Supreme Court has explained that "First Amendment freedoms apply broadly to different types of expression, including art, poetry, film, and music. Such freedoms apply equally to cultured, intellectual expressions and to crude, offensive, or tawdry ones." …

Here, the trial court determined that no violation of Appellant's right to free expression occurred by the admission of the video:

Necessarily, to raise a colorable claim under … the First Amendment …, speech itself must somehow be restricted or sanctioned by the government…. [In this case,] Neither the substantive lyrics nor expressive portrayals contained in the YouTube video at issue served as the basis for any of Appellant's criminal convictions. Saliently, Appellant's conviction for firearms not to be carried without a license did not stem from the depiction of Appellant displaying a firearm in the undated YouTube video. Rather, it was based on the totality of the circumstances indicating his power and intent to control the firearm in the early morning hours of February 20, 2023. The video was properly admitted solely to introduce its non-expressive aspects. Namely, it was highly probative of the fact that Appellant, having apparently constructively possessed the rare purple Glock with a blue laser sight shortly before the carjacking [of Ms. South], was likely to have continued to possess the weapon up to the point at which he discarded the weapon when fleeing from police ten days later. In short, because the artistic expressions contained in [the] video were not regulated or sanctioned by the Commonwealth in the instant matter, the free speech clauses of neither the federal nor the Pennsylvania Constitution were implicated by the admission of th[e] video at trial.

The trial court's reasoning is supported by the record, and its legal conclusion is sound. We conclude the trial court did not err in admitting the video, and Appellant's constitutional right to free expression was not implicated….

#7843. If You Run Social Media for a University, Don't Misprint the Nickname of Its Team

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

From Hinckley v. Univ. of Wyoming, decided Aug. 28 by Judge Scott Skavdahl (D. Wyo.), but just recently posted on Westlaw (appeal pending):

{Unless otherwise noted, these facts are uncontested.} Plaintiff … alleges that she was wrongfully terminated from her employment as a Marketing and Communications Specialist I at University of Wyoming because of her gender and in retaliation for protected workplace conduct….

Shortly after starting in her new role, Plaintiff began to display job performance issues, including being late to work, treating others poorly, and making mistakes. Some of these performance issues may have been due to the lack of oversight and direction supplied by [Marketing Manager] Cattelan, but Cattelan was not Plaintiff's supervisor. Nevertheless, Plaintiff made numerous mistakes that were not a result of Cattelan's lack of guidance or oversight.

For example, in November 2023, Plaintiff was asked to prepare a press release to celebrate a UW Professor who had received a national award. The professor met with Plaintiff, but found Plaintiff's draft inadequate due to "poor writing quality and lack of accuracy." Plaintiff responded combatively to the feedback and the press release was never published.

On December 8, 2023, Plaintiff posted the post [the first one in the image above -EV] to the College of Business' social media (Instagram). The post failed to meet College of Business brand standards and contained a significant spelling error, reading "Go Polks!" instead of "Go Pokes!" (hereinafter, the "first social media error"). Cattelan highlighted this error as particularly concerning given that Plaintiff is an alumna of the University of Wyoming….

For more, you can read the long opinion. But here's the heart of the matter, which is followed by the image that I placed at the top of the post:

Defendant has articulated several legitimate, non-discriminatory reasons for Plaintiff's termination…. Plaintiff fails to show Defendant's stated reasons for terminating her were a mere pretext or that she incurred disparate treatment….

While Plaintiff disputes some of the characterization of these, the vast majority of incidents of Plaintiff's poor job performance are undisputed or admitted. She does not dispute the numerous social media errors were her fault. Plaintiff admits she received the university's brand book and she contends that her work followed the brand and voice of the College of Business.  Yet, no reasonable jury could find her social media posts adhered to COB brand guidelines. The failure to follow the brand guidelines is as simple as "Coca-Cola" versus "Pepsi" [a separate social media error that the court describes elsewhere -EV] or "Polks" v. "Pokes." …

NEXT: If You Commit a Crime with a Gun, You Might Not Want to Use a Purple Gun with a Blue Laser Sight

Eugene Volokh is the Thomas M. Siebel Senior Fellow at the Hoover Institution at Stanford, and the Gary T. Schwartz Distinguished Professor of Law Emeritus and Distinguished Research Professor at UCLA School of Law. Naturally, his posts here (like the opinions of the other bloggers) are his own, and not endorsed by any institution. He is also the co-host of the Free Speech Unmuted podcast.

Indoor air quality monitors can help you breathe easier at home by detecting hazards you can’t see or smell. Gases like radon and carbon monoxide are colorless and odorless but dangerous if inhaled, and these home devices may also identify other pollutants, including volatile organic compounds (VOCs) and airborne particulate matter like dust and pollen. They can serve as a first alert, signaling when to leave an area where the air is unsafe or prompting you to start clearing pollutants and head off health problems. Keep in mind, however, that not all air quality monitors detect all harmful pollutants.

Concerned about the dangers of hidden pollutants lingering in the air of typical homes, we decided to test a number of today’s most popular air quality monitors. We began by extensively researching more than 40 air quality monitors to narrow the field and then selected a range of models to test. (Spoiler: Not all of the air quality monitors we tested earned a spot on this lineup.)

It’s easy to take steps to improve the air quality in your home with an air quality monitor. The best air quality monitor will depend on which pollutants you want to keep track of and whether you prefer a basic or tech-forward model. Our favorite is the Airthings 292 Wave Mini Indoor Air Quality Monitor. It monitors total VOCs (TVOCs), radon, temperature, humidity, mold risk, and outdoor pollen levels. It also comes with smart-home capability and easy-to-use air quality indicators, and it’s suitable for multi-room use.

Ahead, find out what the devices can do and see how the models listed below fared in our hands-on testing to help you choose the best air quality monitor for your home.

Bottom line: Choosing the right air quality monitor depends on specific needs, from detecting VOCs to integrating with smart-home systems.

When it comes to air quality monitors, accuracy is essential. While we didn’t have access to a laboratory for testing, we could offer a measure of control by testing all the monitors under similar situations to see if the readings would correspond when compared to one another. The following monitors all detected the presence of pollutants in our hands-on tests, and we would not hesitate to recommend any of them to help our readers choose a product to detect airborne pollutants in the home.

To measure chemical pollutants in the air without spending a lot, consider the well-priced Wave Mini. The Wave Mini detects TVOCs, humidity, and temperature in the room. After spending a few hours exposed to a dish of oil-based stain in a closed box, the monitor’s TVOC levels spiked. When we compared its temperature and humidity readings to other monitors being tested, the readings were comparable. We believe it accurately portrayed all three readings.

The Wave Mini offers visual indication of air quality in the room, which is accessible when the user waves a hand in front of the monitor. A light flashes green for “healthy,” yellow for “caution,” and red for “poor” air quality.

Users can purchase a hub separately, allowing them to integrate with smart-home products such as Google Assistant and Alexa. The Wave Mini also tracks outdoor pollen levels via the app that syncs with a local weather service. If users don’t have a specific need for monitoring carbon monoxide, radon, or dust, the Wave Mini may be just the right budget-friendly device to keep track of chemical pollutants in the home.

Get the Airthings 292 air quality monitor at Amazon.

Amazon, increasingly offering more of its own brand of products, has entered the air quality monitor field with this device, which measures particulate matter, TVOCs, carbon monoxide, humidity, and temperature. It’s ideal for bedrooms because the small white cube with a little stainless steel vent in front doesn’t have a large display that might keep some folks awake. Instead, a tiny indicator light at the top that shines green, yellow, or red notifies the user of the current air quality. We didn’t find the indicator light to be bright enough to be annoying; it was just bright enough to display the air quality at a glance. However, it only works in a darkened room—it’s not bright enough to see it in sunny daylight.

The Amazon smart air quality monitor syncs with Bluetooth and Wi-Fi, and we found it simple to connect to both. We were unable, however, to connect the monitor to our Echo Show (not included), although it’s advertised as being able to do so. We’re not sure what caused the glitch, since our Echo Show and the monitor individually synced with the Alexa app, but it’s possible it will only connect with newer models of the Echo Show (ours is an older model). Still, the Alexa app on our smartphone provided excellent real-time readings and charts that made it easy to see the air quality.

We tested this monitor in our test box for VOCs and particulate matter. For the first test, we put a dish of oil-based stain in the box, gave it a couple of hours to infiltrate the air, and then checked the app. The VOC reading had spiked. We then opened the box to check the monitor—the indicator light shone red (hazardous air quality). For the second test, we shook the dust mop over the box and monitored the app on our phone. The PM2.5 reading spiked in about 5 minutes and fell 20 minutes later as the dust settled.

To test the CO sensor, we put the monitor in the garage, started the car, and closed the doors. We watched on our smartphone as the CO reading on the app rose. When we opened the garage door, the indicator light was red. We brought the monitor out into the fresh air, and the light turned green in about 10 minutes.

Compared with the other monitors we tested, the Amazon smart air quality monitor’s temperature and humidity readings were right on target. Overall, we liked this little monitor, and we felt it was accurate and discreet enough not to detract from bedroom or nursery decor.

Get the Amazon air quality monitor at Amazon.

This monitor was quite an overachiever in our testing! It connects using Bluetooth technology via the Airthings app and provided detailed reports about our home’s air quality. It will also connect to smart-home devices, such as Alexa, but not via Wi-Fi. Instead, users must download the IFTTT app for their smartphone, which allows a connection between Wave Plus and Alexa.

The first test we performed on the Wave Plus was in a friend’s home where radon was previously detected and is being treated. They have a professional radon detector, so we wanted to see if the Wave Plus would also detect the gas. We positioned it in the basement of the home and left it there for a week.

On our return, we checked the Airthings app and found a radon reading of 3.5pCi/L. This was the exact reading the professional radon detector was showing. When we waved a hand in front of the Wave Plus, it flashed a yellow light that told us the air quality was affected but not hazardous. When we took the Wave Plus outside in the fresh air, the radon level dropped, and the light turned green to indicate healthy air.

We then tested the Wave Plus in our test box where we exposed it for 2 hours to a dish of oil-based stain, a product that contains VOCs. When we checked the monitor, the light was red (indicating hazardous air quality), and on the app we saw that the TVOC reading had spiked. We also compared the monitor’s temperature and humidity readings to those of the other monitors, which were consistent.

We performed one more test—a very unscientific CO2 test. We know that smoke contains CO2, so we took the Wave Plus to the garage and put it on a bench. We used our beehive smoker to blow little puffs of smoke directly on the monitor. The CO2 levels on the app increased slightly, and the indicator light turned yellow. We felt it was detecting some CO2, but we couldn’t tell if it was sensing as much as it should have been. Still, it registered an increase similar to the CO2 detectors on other monitors, so we felt the smoke from the beehive smoker didn’t contain much carbon dioxide.

Get the Airthings 2950 air quality monitor at Amazon or The Home Depot.

The AirVisual Pro air quality monitor by IQAir boasts advanced laser technology, airflow control, and a crafted calibration algorithm to detect precise particulate matter and CO2 data. We felt the most important readings on this monitor for allergy sufferers were the PM1, PM2.5, and PM10 readings. These sensors detect various-size airborne particles, ranging from pollen, which is rather large and can be detected by the PM10 sensor, all the way down to ultrafine dust that can’t be seen but is easily inhaled.

The AirVisual Pro syncs with smart-home systems using either Wi-Fi or IFTTT. We tested both, and both worked well. The best thing about this monitor is its large visual display screen. It’s nice to be able to check the app, but in our opinion, it’s even better to see a visual display at a glance without having to use a smartphone first. Another plus: This monitor gathers outside air quality ratings via local weather reports and displays them prominently.

When we put the AirVisual monitor in our test box and shook a dust mop over it, all three PM sensor readings spiked, which indicated that it was detecting a range of particulate matter sizes. After 30 minutes, the PM10 and PM2.5 readings dropped, as we suspected they would, because the dust had settled. However, the PM1 reading only declined slightly, which we think was due to the extra-tiny particulates that remained airborne longer. The PM1 reading didn’t drop for another hour.

The air quality monitor also detectsCO2 levels, temperature, and humidity. We tested the CO2 sensor by putting the monitor in the garage and blowing puffs of smoke on it from our beehive smoker. The CO2 readings increased slightly, but they didn’t spike. Still, that was consistent with our other monitor tests for CO2.

This specific monitor had some trouble with temperature and humidity, as both readings were off by more than 7 degrees Fahrenheit/points compared to the other monitors. Also, it doesn’t detect VOCs. Overall, this is a handy monitor to detect the presence of primary allergy triggers, such as airborne particulates.

Get the IQAir air quality monitor at Amazon or Walmart.

Those looking for a portable air quality monitor to detect pollen and other airborne particulate matter may find the Temtop P600 air quality monitor to be just the ticket. It uses a Quantum Semiconductor International (QSI) laser diode to detect particulate matter as small as 2.5 microns. A highly sensitive diode also found in professional laboratory equipment, it also detects larger particulates, such as pollen, in the 10-micron range.

The unit has a kickstand that folds out, so users can stand the monitor on a table, nightstand, or even a tent floor when camping out. The first thing we did was charge it fully using the included USB cord, then we started testing.

There wasn’t too much to test on this one, however, since the P600 detects only airborne particulate matter. We put it in our test box and shook a dust mop over it. This monitor doesn’t sync with smart devices, so we couldn’t monitor the readings remotely from a smartphone. Instead, we checked it every few minutes to see if it had changed. The readings predictably spiked after 10 minutes and then gradually dropped (after about 25 minutes) as the dust settled.

One of the upsides to this Temtop model is that it displays air quality over 12 hours on a chart readout. This helped us see air quality changes over the course of a day. Unfortunately, the battery runs down pretty quickly—we had to charge it every morning for a couple of hours in order for it to run the rest of the day. The alternative is to leave it plugged into the USB cord, but the cord plugs into the bottom of the monitor so it won’t sit upright when plugged in. As a solution, we recommend turning the monitor on periodically to check the air quality in a room and then turning it back off to save battery life.

Get the Temtop P600 air quality monitor at Amazon.

Before we chose monitors for hands-on testing, we researched more than 40 models, looking for various sensor types and paying close attention to buyers’ reviews and ratings. We also reached out to an industry expert to get some additional insight. Lisa Townley, the associate director of product management/replacement parts at Carrier, a global provider of HVAC solutions, says, “As people are focused on the health of their indoor environments more than ever before, it’s imperative that they take steps to improve their living and working spaces, including the air they breathe.” She goes on to say that knowing what’s in your air is important because you can “take steps to lower the likelihood of mold … better manage allergens and asthma triggers … and create conditions for improved sleep.” She adds that air monitors with advanced technology to detect finer particles down to 2.5 microns or smaller are particularly useful in the home. We took this expert advice into consideration when choosing which products to test.

For our actual tests—and we must say right off the bat that these were not scientifically controlled trials—we created situations we felt mimicked (or exceeded) real-life air quality problems. To test whether monitors with particulate matter (PM) sensors worked, we put them in a large box and shook a very dirty dust mop over the top. We then monitored the PM readouts on smartphones (or manually) to see when or if they spiked and when they fell (as the dust settled).

We used wood stain, which contains VOCs, including formaldehyde, to test the monitors with VOC sensors. We placed an open dish of oil-based wood stain in the test box and allowed the fumes to infiltrate the box for a couple of hours before checking the readings.

We got a little more creative when testing other sensors! We tested monitors with carbon dioxide (CO2) sensors by blowing puffs of smoke directly on the monitors using our beehive smoker. We tested for carbon monoxide (CO) by putting the monitors with CO detectors in a closed garage with a car running inside. We tested a single monitor to see if it would detect nitrogen dioxide (NO2) by starting a wood fire in the fireplace of our she shed and then closing the flue and monitoring the readout on our smartphone.

To see how well radon sensors worked, we tested them in the basement of a friend’s home, where we already knew radon was an issue.

Temperature and humidity were casually tested by comparing those numbers with other monitors and using the average of the readings (minus the highest and lowest, which we threw out) to determine consistency.

We looked for readout increases and decreases but didn’t compare actual numbers. The detection numbers varied from monitor to monitor from the start, and we felt that one monitor might receive more exposure to a pollutant than another, even though we tried to keep the exposure levels similar. If the readings more than doubled, we deemed it a “spike.”

We also examined and analyzed how easy it was to sync the monitors with Bluetooth; Wi-Fi; or If This, Then That (IFTTT) capability.

To arrive at our awards, we gave models points using a rubric—the better we felt the monitor performed during a test, the more points it received. At the end of testing, we added the points and used them to determine the best category for each monitor.

The monitors we tested ranged from single-pollutant sensors, such as simple radon detectors, to multiple-pollutant detection models that tracked the e humidity levels and several toxic gases. In most cases, a consumer will want a monitor that detects the type of air pollution that puts their home and family at the most significant risk.

For example, consumers who live in a region with known radon problems will want to look for a radon detector or a carbon monoxide detector if they’re concerned about automobile exhaust fumes seeping in from an attached garage. In addition, the following factors are important considerations for consumers shopping for an air quality monitor.

Consumer-quality monitors are not as precise as laboratory detectors, but they’re typically good enough to alert household members that airborne particulates and toxic gases are present.

Monitors that detect dangerous gases, such as VOCs and carbon monoxide, feature electrochemical sensors that react to the presence of gaseous toxins in the air. In some monitors, these sensors must be manually calibrated, but many of the newer models are precalibrated.

Monitors designed to detect dust, allergens, and other airborne particulates do so by estimating the amount of particulate matter that passes in front of a laser. Though valuable, these measurements may not be exact for two main reasons: larger PM might not drift into the laser chamber, and the laser might overlook the tiniest PM.

Home air quality monitors can detect a range of pollutants and will generally detect one or more of the following. Some may detect additional contaminants, but these are the most common.

While some air quality monitors are relatively straightforward, others are pretty high-tech. For example, some models are Wi-Fi capable, and others connect to smartphones and devices via Bluetooth capability or IFTTT technology. Such monitors come with apps that can be downloaded to a smartphone, and then the app walks users through the installation process.

Single-pollutant detectors, such as carbon monoxide detectors, are among the simplest to use because they often just plug into an outlet. If they detect the gas in question, they emit a high-pitched alarm. The best air quality monitor for any individual should be easy to use, depending on the person’s technical skill level. Consumers will want to avoid choosing a complex model with a huge learning curve that requires watching online videos for hours just to figure out how it operates.

Most air quality monitors are relatively small devices, with a sensor unit and a screen that displays how much of the pollutant is currently in the air. Portable units, which fit in a tool belt, purse, or tool bag, are the smallest of all. These are well suited for testing the air on jobsites or in rental homes that don’t have stationary monitors.

Many monitors have the ability to detect numerous problem gases and pollutants and are suitable for multiple spaces. Those who want air quality monitoring to integrate with smart-home technology—so it can display information on a phone or respond to voice commands—will want to look for a smart air quality monitor.

Some people prefer visual alerts rather than numbers or charts that can be challenging to decipher. Today’s monitors often provide color-coded lights that indicate air quality at a glance. Typically, a green light indicates good air quality, a yellow light signifies the air quality is less than optimal but not dangerous, and a red light is a warning that the air quality is poor.

Response time refers to how quickly an air quality monitor will sense the problem and alert the household. Higher-quality devices often have quicker response times because their sensors are more accurate. Response times will also vary depending on which pollutant the monitor is tracking.

For example, some carbon monoxide monitors will sound an alarm after detecting a low level of gas over a few hours; however, if they detect a higher level, the monitor will sound the alarm after just a few minutes. Monitors that measure dust and pollen may not emit a warning at all but simply track and record the varying levels of the pollutants by the hour.

Air quality monitors are either corded (running on electricity from a standard household outlet) or battery-operated (powered by rechargeable batteries). Both are efficient, but for those who need to test air quality in a storage shed or another remote location, a battery-operated model is the handiest.

Very few things are as important as the quality of the air your family is breathing. If you’re new to air quality monitors, you likely have some questions.

According to SmartAir, a developer of air filtration products, the accuracy of air quality readings on monitors falls between 70 percent and 85 percent. While most monitors are as accurate as possible, no single model is 100 percent accurate.

The most common pollutants are airborne particulate matter, such as dust, pet dander, and pollen. However, some other airborne irritants to be aware of are carbon monoxide, lead, radon, and carbon dioxide.

A few simple ideas can improve poor air quality:Clean regularlyKeep your home well ventilatedPurchase an air purifierMaintain your heating and cooling systemsAdd house plantsClean air ductsClean regularlyKeep your home well ventilatedPurchase an air purifierMaintain your heating and cooling systemsAdd house plantsClean air ducts

They sense high or unhealthy levels of particulate matter or toxic gases and alert residents if the levels become dangerous. Many options on the market rely on color-coded air quality indicators to alert users as to the status of the air quality.

Most consumer models can’t detect mold. However, consumers can purchase a home mold test with a petri dish and ingredients that will trigger mold growth if the home has a mold problem. While growing mold may seem counterproductive, it allows consumers to discover whether mold spores are present in the air, so they can take steps to locate the source of the mold and get rid of it.

We began by charging the batteries overnight to ensure every pair was ready for a full day of evaluation. We also wore each pair while shoveling, walking the dog, and using our phones to see how they handled real tasks. Finally, we ran them on low until the batteries died to find the true maximum runtime.

While dependable heat is the primary goal—especially when you’re trying to stay warm without heat—heated gloves must balance insulation with the specific demands of your environment and activities.

Your planned activities will dictate whether you need a heavy-duty glove or a slim liner. For winter sports like skiing or snowmobiling, gloves with a rugged, wind- and waterproof shell will be essential. If you need winter work gloves, a pair with leather palms offers a secure grip. To use your phone or complete detailed tasks, a thin, touchscreen-compatible liner may be the best choice.

Since there’s no universal glove sizing, be sure to measure your hands before buying. When trying the gloves on, your fingers should almost (but not quite) touch the ends, and the wrist cuff should extend far enough to tuck into your jacket sleeves to prevent cold air and moisture from slipping in.

For maximum heat retention and comfort, look for a windproof shell (often made from a polyester blend) combined with a soft interior liner (generally fleece). If you’ll be doing heavy-duty tasks that require a good grip, seek out a pair with durable leather palms and fingertips. Also, be aware that more insulation and padding equal more warmth, but thickness comes at the cost of dexterity.

If your winter activities involve direct contact with snow or ice, waterproofing is essential. Manufacturers typically use synthetic shells made from polyester or nylon to prevent moisture from soaking through. However, complete waterproofing can trap sweat inside, leading to a clammy or uncomfortable feel. To counter this, you may want a pair with a waterproof palm and a ventilated back.

As with heated vests and jackets, most electric heated gloves rely on small rechargeable lithium-ion batteries to provide warmth for anywhere from 2 to 8 hours. If you want heat that lasts through a full day of work or sport, consider buying gloves with removable batteries so you can swap in another set once the first ones become depleted.

While heated gloves have been around for a couple of decades, advancements in battery technology and weather-resistant materials have made them more effective and less bulky. Still, many people have never used heated gloves, so it’s common to have questions. Here are answers to the most frequent inquiries to help you get the most out of these winter workwear essentials.

Yes, heated gloves are worth it if you spend significant time in the cold, have poor circulation, or do outdoor work where maintaining hand dexterity and comfort matters.

Yes, heated gloves are generally safe since they run on low-voltage batteries and include protections like temperature controls and sometimes auto‑shutoff. However, you should stop using them if you feel burning or notice damage to the wiring or battery.

Yes, many heated gloves are machine washable, though you’ll want to check the care tag for specific instructions. Some models require hand-washing, and others can only be wiped down with a damp cloth. Regardless of the method, avoid wringing them out to prevent damage to their internal heating wires.

Many battery-heated gloves can stay warm for up to 8 hours on low before needing a recharge. However, because lithium-ion batteries tend to gradually weaken, you may see battery life decrease as time goes by. Generally speaking, you can charge a typical lithium-ion battery 300 to 500 times before needing to replace it.

Heated gloves should fit snugly but not be restrictive. Your fingers should almost touch the ends, and the wrist cuff should be long enough to tuck into your sleeves. A fit that’s too tight can compress the heating elements and restrict circulation, while a fit that is too loose allows heat to escape.

Most heated gloves warm up within 1 to 5 minutes, depending on the battery voltage and heat setting. Many are designed to get warm quickly on high before being turned down to maintain comfort and preserve battery life.

It depends. Heated gloves are better if you need warmth across your whole hand for extended periods or active use—though they are more expensive. Cheaper disposable or rechargeable hand warmers may be sufficient if all you need is pocket warmth, but they’re really only meant for short outings.

#7840. Arkansas S. Ct.: Legislature May Revive Cases Barred by Statute of Limitations

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

The court reverses its precedent, dating back to 1846, that held such revival unconstitutionally restricted the defendant's "vested rights" not to be sued, which had been created by the earlier statute of limitations.

From H.C. v. Nesmith, decided last week by the Arkansas Supreme Court, in an opinion by Justice Nicholas Bronni, joined by Justices Courtney Rae Hudson, Cody Hiland, and Rhonda Wood (note that other state courts are split on this question, see, e.g., this post and this one):

This case presents a particularly important question: Can the General Assembly extend the statute of limitations in cases where it has already run and afford child-sex-abuse victims an opportunity to hold their abusers accountable? … [T]his court's vested-rights precedent … categorically bars "expand[ing] a limitation period so as to revive a claim already barred." …

Revisiting our vested-rights precedent, we conclude that it lacks any constitutional basis and, as such, cannot stand. We therefore overrule our prior cases prohibiting the legislature from expanding a limitations period and thereby reviving time-barred claims [and] uphold the Vulnerable Victims of Sex Abuse Act against Nesmith's constitutional challenge ….

[Under] our vested-rights precedent …, "the legislature cannot expand a statute of limitation so as to revive a cause of action already barred." That doctrine rests on the assumption that when a civil statute of limitations runs, a tortfeasor has a vested right to the property that could have been the subject of a potential claim….

[But] our cases do not cite any constitutional basis for that doctrine. Far from it, when we first employed that principle to strike down legislation in 1933, we instead relied on a single legal encyclopedia published in 1915 assuring us that—at that sole moment in time—most jurisdictions held that legislatures could not revive a claim after a statute-of-limitations defense had run. Or, perhaps more generously, we relied on that legal encyclopedia plus an unreasoned extension of this court's prior case law suggesting that to retroactively alter an applicable statute of limitations, the legislature needed to speak clearly and show it had considered the consequences. That approach, unbound by actual text or constitutional history, is not consistent with our constitutional role….

To be sure, some later cases—perhaps recognizing that our earlier cases do not cite any constitutional language supporting our vested-rights precedent—suggest that precedent rests on due-process principles…. [But] that label does not work because the expiration of a statute-of-limitations period does not confer a property right—or any other right for that matter.

As the Supreme Court has explained in rejecting similar arguments under the federal due process clause, a statute-of-limitations period merely governs the time within which a claim must be brought, see Chase Sec. Corp. v. Donaldson (1945); it does not reflect a legislative judgment "that [a] defendant should 'be free from liability after the legislatively determined period of time.'" Instead, these limitations "are by definition arbitrary" and rest entirely on legislative judgments about how best to encourage plaintiffs to diligently pursue claims and avoid litigation "after memories have faded, witnesses have died or disappeared, and evidence has been lost."

As such, they "represent a public policy [choice] about" how to balance those interests and exist only by "legislative grace." Altering that period and establishing a different, equally "arbitrary" date does not—contrary to our prior case law's unfounded assertion—deprive a defendant of any vested property right. Rather, balancing competing interests and "resolv[ing] the debate" about when a claim should be time-barred is precisely the kind of thing that our constitution leaves "to the legislature."

We therefore hold that the court's vested-rights precedent has no basis in law, and we overrule our prior cases categorically barring the legislature from expanding the limitations period and thereby reviving claims. Indeed, as we recently reaffirmed, "we are bound by constitutional text," not precedent that "treats our constitution not as a written document but as a set of civic values and norms determined by judges." And we now restore to the General Assembly its constitutional power to decide how long is too long to bring a claim….

Recognizing the vital importance of stare decisis, I nonetheless conclude that this is an exceptional case that warrants breaking with our precedent. Before the General Assembly enacted the Justice for Vulnerable Victims of Sexual Abuse Act, victims of sexual abuse who were under age twenty-one generally had until three years after attaining full age to file suit. Yet childhood sexual abuse presents a unique problem in that—by its very nature—it often prevents victims from bringing timely claims. This consideration leads me to conclude that great injury and injustice will result if we continue to follow our vested-rights precedent in this case….

In recent years, research has revealed the prevalence of childhood sexual abuse and some of the reasons for delayed reporting. For example, we now know that at least one in four girls and one in twenty boys in the United States experience child sexual abuse. Even still, childhood sexual abuse is vastly underreported, and when it is reported, often years or decades have passed. Victims may be reluctant to come forward due to the negative repercussions of disclosure, such as disruptions in family stability, loss of close relationships, or involvement with the authorities; fear of not being believed; and psychological obstacles such as shame and self-blame….

I disagree with the majority's decision to upend 180 years of this court's precedent prohibiting legislative attempts to revive expired statutes of limitation…. In my view, applying our vested-rights precedent to the present case, … the legislature lacked the power to revive the expired statute of limitations applicable to Nesmith, and therefore, the claims against Nesmith were time-barred.

[I]n 1846 this court in Couch v. McKee treated the completed bar [of the statute of limitations] as a property interest that cannot be removed by later legislation. When the statute has run, the defendant's right to be free from the claim becomes part of his or her protected legal estate, an interest the State cannot simply reassign by retroactive enactment. Our later cases have repeatedly applied that same rule, holding that revival statutes cannot constitutionally divest a defendant of a vested limitations defense.

Nor, contrary to the majority's assertion, is our vested-rights jurisprudence untethered from constitutional text. The Arkansas Constitution reflects a longstanding hostility toward retroactive laws impairing settled rights. See Ark. Const. art. 2, § 17 (prohibiting ex post facto laws and laws impairing contractual obligations); id. § 21 (protecting due process). Consistent with those principles, this court has repeatedly recognized that retroactive legislation may not constitutionally disturb vested substantive rights….

That rule is not a mere formalism. Statutes of limitation serve an important public function. They encourage the prompt filing of claims so that the truth-finding process is not impaired by faded memories, lost documents, unavailable records, and deceased witnesses. Those concerns are not hypothetical. The amicus brief filed in this case illustrates the serious prejudice that can result when claims are revived decades after the fact.

Ms. Shirley Suhl, an eighty-seven-year-old retired widow, represents that she is defending claims in federal court arising from alleged events at a facility that ceased operating around 2006 and from conduct dating back nearly forty years. She is not alleged to have personally committed sexual abuse; rather, she is alleged to have known of or been complicit in abuse by others. According to her brief, relevant facility records no longer exist, potential witnesses are elderly or deceased, and one named former employee accused of abuse is now in his nineties. Whether those allegations ultimately have merit is not before us. The point is more basic: the passage of decades can make a fair defense difficult, sometimes impossible.

This is precisely why Arkansas law has treated an accrued limitations defense as vested. Once the limitations period has run, the defendant is entitled to repose, not because the underlying allegations are unimportant but because the law recognizes that, at some point, the defense of stale claims becomes too impaired to permit reliable adjudication. The majority treats the limitations bar as a revocable act of legislative grace. Our cases have treated it differently. They have recognized that once the bar attaches, it becomes a substantive right to resist enforcement of the claim. That rule does not deny the gravity of child sexual abuse. It enforces the constitutional limit on retroactive legislation that destroys vested rights.

In this instance, stare decisis carries particular force. The rule the majority abandons today is not isolated or recently decided precedent. It can be traced back to this court's earliest jurisprudence and has been reaffirmed across generations of cases. Litigants, lawyers, and the General Assembly have long operated against that settled backdrop. Yet today, the majority discards nearly two centuries of precedent. Stability in the law matters, especially when the court alters longstanding rules governing substantive rights and retroactive legislation….

{While many judges and justices pledge full allegiance to the doctrine of stare decisis, even to the point of perpetuating clear errors of constitutional interpretation, I am not one of them. And while it is an important piece of our judicial system, I have frequently noted that "[t]his court "should not invoke stare decisis to uphold precedents that are demonstrably erroneous." Here, however, our two centuries of case law on the subject are rooted in the Arkansas Constitution as article 2 section 21 supports our precedent. Accordingly, I would follow it.

Joshua D. Gillispie (Gillispie Law Firm) and Brian G. Brooks represent plaintiffs.

#7837. Ukrainian National Sentenced for Role in Hacking Hospitals, Businesses, and Governments as Part of Ransomware Conspiracies Causing Over $100 Million in Losses

An official website of the United States government

Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( Lock Locked padlock ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

Artem Stryzhak, 36, a Ukrainian national, was sentenced today to 70 months in prison for conspiracy to commit computer fraud in connection with a series of ransomware attacks that targeted hospitals, government entities, law firms, and other businesses around the world.

“This sentence concludes a years-long, multi-continent investigation into a defendant who participated in cyber-attacks against Americans’ businesses and health care,” said Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the Justice Department’s Criminal Division. “Cybercriminals who terrorize American businesses cannot evade justice by operating from abroad or hiding behind sophisticated technology. Artem Stryzhak’s sentence underscores the Justice Department’s resolve to dismantle ransomware groups, hold them accountable, and protect American businesses and people from cyber extortion.”

“Ransomware attacks like those committed by the defendant wreak enormous havoc — harming victim companies that pay millions in remediation and ransoms, preventing hospitals and other critical facilities from accessing data, and putting sensitive information in the hands of bad actors,” said U.S. Attorney Joseph Nocella Jr. for the Eastern District of New York. “Today’s sentence reflects that cybercriminals cannot hide from law enforcement and will face significant punishment for their criminal conduct. We remain determined to capture Volodymyr Tymoshchuk, a serial ransomware developer and Stryzhak’s co-conspirator.”

“Disrupting a ransomware group that attacked approximately 1,500 victims worldwide and sentencing a defendant who had targeted healthcare during the COVID-19 pandemic is of significant importance to this office,” said U.S. Attorney Gregory W. Kehoe for the Middle District of Florida. “We are proud of our law enforcement partners for their skilled investigative work in bringing this criminal to justice.”

“Artem Stryzhak is a prolific cybercriminal who worked with multiple ransomware groups to target U.S. businesses and hospitals,” said Operations Director Brett Leatherman of the FBI’s Cyber Branch. “These groups disrupted patient care and caused more than $100 million in losses. Today’s sentence reflects the seriousness of Stryzhak’s crimes and demonstrates the FBI’s global reach and extensive network of international partners. Multiple field offices contributed to this investigation, and our work does not end here. We will continue to leverage every tool at our disposal to track down Stryzhak’s co-conspirators and hold them accountable, including Volodymyr Viktorovych Tymoshchuk.”

According to court documents, Stryzhak, formerly of Barcelona, Spain, conspired with others to perpetrate ransomware attacks on behalf of multiple ransomware groups against victim computer networks in the United States and other countries. The conspiracies caused significant damage to victim computer systems. Beginning in approximately June 2021, Stryzhak joined the ongoing Nefilim conspiracy as a Nefilim ransomware affiliate.  Stryzhak was given access to the Nefilim ransomware and agreed with one of the Nefilim ransomware group administrators, Volodymyr Tymoshchuk, to pay the Nefilim administrators, including Tymoshchuk, 20% of the ransom proceeds extorted from victims in exchange for Stryzhak’s access to the Nefilim ransomware.

The ransomware attacks that Stryzhak conducted with Nefilim ransomware included a June 2021 attack in which Stryzhak stole data from a company in the oil and gas transportation industry. About a week later, Stryzhak created email addresses that were incorporated in a ransom note sent to the victim company. Stryzhak conspired with the Nefilim ransomware actors until at least October 2021. If a victim paid the ransom demand, the perpetrators provided the decryption key, enabling the victim to decrypt files locked by the ransomware.

Also according to court documents, Stryzhak separately joined the Hive ransomware group as one of its earliest affiliates. From June 2021 to January 2023, Hive conspirators attacked approximately 1,500 victims worldwide, including government entities, hospitals, and businesses. Hive ransomware attacks caused major disruptions in victim daily operations around the world and affected responses to the COVID-19 pandemic. In one case, a hospital attacked by the Hive ransomware group had to forgo digital technology to treat existing patients and was unable to accept new patients immediately following the attack.

In his role as a Hive affiliate, Stryzhak and his co-conspirators deployed Hive ransomware against seven victims, including law firms, a dentist office, and a healthcare provider during the COVID-19 pandemic. Victims were unable to access their encrypted data. The FBI, as part of a months-long disruption campaign against the Hive ransomware group, provided a decryption key to one of Stryzhak’s victims, thereby allowing that victim to decrypt its encrypted data without having to pay a ransom.

Stryzhak was arrested in Spain in June 2024 and extradited to the United States in April 2025. Stryzhak pleaded guilty in December 2025 to two counts of conspiracy to commit fraud, extortion, and related activity in connection with computers.

The FBI Springfield Field Office investigated the Nefilim ransomware case and the FBI Tampa Field Office investigated the Hive ransomware case. The Criminal Division’s Office of International Affairs, the FBI’s New York Field Office, and Spanish law enforcement authorities provided substantial assistance locating, arresting, and extraditing Stryzhak.

Acting Assistant Deputy Chief James S. Yoon of the Criminal Division’s Computer Crime and Intellectual Property Section (CCIPS), former CCIPS Senior Trial Attorney Brian Z. Mund, and Assistant United States Attorneys Alexander F. Mindlin and Ellen H. Sise of the Eastern District of New York’s National Security and Cybercrime Section prosecuted the Nefilim ransomware case. CCIPS Trial Attorneys Alison M. Zitron and Christen M. Gallagher and Assistant United States Attorney Hannah Watson of the Middle District of Florida prosecuted the Hive ransomware case.

The U.S. Department of State’s Transnational Organized Crime (TOC) Rewards Program has offered a reward of up to $11 million for information leading to the arrest and/or conviction or location of Stryzhak’s charged co-conspirator, Volodymyr Tymoshchuk. Anyone with information about Tymoshchuk should contact the FBI via phone at +1-917-242-1407, by email at TymoTips@fbi.gov, by contacting your local field office, if in the United States, or by contacting the nearest U.S. Embassy, if located overseas. More information about the Tymoshchuk TOC reward offer and one related to Hive ransomware is located on the State Department website.

CCIPS investigates and prosecutes cybercrime and intellectual property (IP) crime in coordination with domestic and international law enforcement agencies, often with assistance from the private sector. Since 2020, CCIPS has secured the conviction of over 180 cyber and IP criminals, and court orders for the return of over $350 million in victim funds.

#7836. Back At The Mayflower

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

The first day of the 2026 Federalist Society Convention is in the can. There is much to report.

First, it is good to be back at the Mayflower--well at least good for those of us who made it in. Several years ago, FedSoc decided to move from the Mayflower to the Hilton, a much larger venue. The group had simply outgrown the classic hotel. The downside, of course, is that the Hilton is a terrible hotel. There were assassination attempts on two Presidents at the "Hinkley Hilton." There was no common meeting area, and attendees had to traverse a labyrinth of hallways between sessions. Worse, the rooms were a decade overdue for renovation. We hated it. But most of us were able to fit in.

This year, the registration for the national convention filled up almost instantaneously. I had planned to bring many of my students, but they simply never made it off the waiting list. Longtime members were hanging out in the lobby, hoping to make it off the waiting list, with no luck. I heard that the Harvard FedSoc chapter scheduled a conference for students who could not get in--apparently known as the "shadow docket." People complained to me, as if it was my fault we went back to the small Mayflower because of my carping about the Hilton. I get blamed for everything.

FedSoc will have to figure out what to do for next year, the 40th Anniversary of the National Lawyers Convention. We could always try to check out the new East Wing Ballroom, assuming Judge Leon doesn't enjoin it! The Gaylord Hotel in Maryland could fit everyone, but I am still scarred from the gala dinner there in 2016. I have long been a fan of holding the convention outside of D.C. It would send the exact right message. The times where people in D.C. offices can just stop by for a few panels are long gone. (The sold out registration means only those willing to attend the entire program will be there.) And anyone who wants to speak on the program of this platform should be willing to get on a flight. I would have recommended Texas for the venue, but we will soon be in hostile territory. Perhaps the free state of Florida is the last, best hope.

Second, the format of the FedSoc conference is different. I was so accustomed to the usual rhythm, I feel a bit disoriented. There are no breakout panels. Every panel is a "showcase" panel in the Grand Ballroom. The other rooms are overflow rooms with screens to watch the programming. The schedule is all different. The Rosenkranz Debate was on Thursday afternoon rather than Saturday afternoon over lunch. The Bork and Olson Lectures are both on Friday. And the program ends on Saturday at 2:15, about three hours earlier than usual. Also, instead of having lunchtime panels, all of the rooms on the second floor host smaller, intimate lunches. You could sit at a table with a judge and eight others to chat about an interesting topic. I was at Chief Judge Elrod's table to learn about the Lord of the Rings. (Trigger warning for commenters: I have never read any of those books, I fell asleep during the first movie, and never watched the others.) The discussion was fun! There are some judges who treat their judicial sinecures like Gollum treats the ring. How precious.

I see pros and cons to the new format. On the plus side, this format was far less overwhelming. I routinely felt drained by all of the content. Also, I always felt like I was missing something when I committed to a panel. As a result, I would often bounce between different panels, ensuring that I missed stuff. On the negative side, I enjoyed the ability to pick different panels that may be of interest. I thought the practice groups put on a wide arrange of topical panels. Moreover, there are far fewer speaking slots available with only a few panels each day. These are prime opportunities for up-and-coming members. Still, for this America 250 celebration, I liked the theme in which each panel was framed around a few words from the Declaration. This is an area I have studied for years, and I still learned quite a lot. I don't think we could have kept the Declaration theme going with breakouts.

Third, there is a much stronger focus on students--the lifeblood of Fedsoc. I appreciated that each panel was introduced by a student, rather than the chair of the practice group. During the Scalia dinner, the winners of the Feddie student chapter awards were asked to stand up. I am so proud of the South Texas Chapter, and my students Ryan Lanier and Makayla Arthur, for winning the Hamilton Award for "Most Improved Chapter." Matthew Weinberg, the President of the UCLA chapter during the Percival protest, was given a courage award. And each of the Soc! lunchtime tables was hosted by a student chapter leader.

We can never forget that FedSoc was founded by a bunch of law students. Old people (present company included) need to always give the youth these sorts of opportunities. It wasn't that long ago that I met Will Scharf at the Mayflower, and now he is White House Counsel. I can say the same for so many current judges and other officials that I met when I was student. Indeed, some of the current judges hosted me as a Professor at their chapters! (In 2033, I'll be 49.)  Everything that rises must converge.

Fourth, the decoration of the Mayflower and the Marriott Marquis ballroom was top-notch. There is red, white, and blue bunting all over the Grand Ballroom. The backdrop of the Scalia dinner was expertly done, topped off with George Washington's bible! (No, we couldn't touch it.) The Marine Corp band played during the processional. The Madison Club reception was no longer crammed into a tiny, dark, and noisy tent. It was held in a spacious atrium at the Marquis. Moreover, Madison Club members have access to Edgar's as a lounge to get food and snacks during the day. What a really, really smart idea. This sort of attention to detail matters, at least to me.

Fifth the security is intense. Registration is now available on the lower level. No one is allowed into the hallway without showing credentials and passing through a body scanner. Large bags are banned and smaller bags are searched. The busses from the Mayflower to the Marquis were swept for security, and there was a National Guardsman on board. It is a sad commentary that we have to take these precautions. But with an actual assassination attempt against Justice Kavanaugh, I think we have to accept these costs. (During the Scalia Dinner, Justice Alito praised the courage of Justices Kavanaugh and Barrett for joining the Dobbs decision, knowing what risks that could bring.)

Sixth, I was sort of expecting the vibe at the Mayflower to be grim in light of last week's election. I remember how the 2008 convention felt something like a funeral. I think the mood was mostly one of shock. There are efforts in play to figure out how to deal with the loss of Attorneys General in Texas, Ohio, Iowa, and Kansas. Other states will have to pick up the heavy lifting. Lawyers in Austin can find safe refuge in Baton Rouge, Jackson, St. Louis, Nashville, Tallahassee, Montgomery, and other cities. I am currently researching the laws of intervention on both the plaintiff and defendant side, confessions of error in criminal cases, as well as standing for state legislators and the state senate. The agenda has shifted.

Seventh, one thing I love about the National Convention is that business is conducted right in the hallways. There is a strong sentiment to do everything we can to confirm the remaining judges. These aren't quite the midnight judges of the outgoing Federalist Party, but we are in a similar mindset. There is a universal agreement that Judge Rudofsky was screwed. I second everything my friend Rob Luther wrote in this op-ed in the Arkansas newspaper. And there is a concerted effort to help Elliot Gaiser get across the finish line. What a complete waste if this seat is left for James Talarico to fill. Talk about cutting off your nose to spite your six-gendered face. And then there's Todd Butler. Had the election turned out differently, things may have gone differently. But he is on the path to confirmation. I hope Butler proves me wrong--and he will have a quick opportunity to do so. The January en banc siting has a huge 922(g) case and a challenge to Texas's social media law. As for the new Eighth Circuit nominee, Cody Hiland, he have to prove a lot of people wrong.

#7835. National Security Division Announces First “Near Miss” Non-Prosecution Agreement Under the Department-wide Corporate Enforcement Policy

An official website of the United States government

Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( Lock Locked padlock ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

The Department of Justice announced today that it has entered into a non-prosecution agreement with Extreme Networks, Inc.  The company agreed to pay criminal penalties totaling $975,721.84 to resolve the Department’s investigation of sanctions and export control offenses.

The Department reached the agreement under its 2026 Corporate Enforcement and Voluntary Self-Disclosure Policy (“the Policy”), which incentivizes companies to voluntarily disclose discovered misconduct, cooperate with Department investigations, and timely and appropriately remediate the wrongdoing.

This agreement with Extreme Networks marks the Department’s first non-prosecution agreement in a “near-miss” case under the Policy, meaning a case that involved full cooperation and appropriate remediation but did not qualify for a declination of prosecution.  While Extreme Networks’ disclosure to the National Security Division (NSD) was not timely because it occurred under imminent threat of disclosure by a news publication, Extreme Networks nonetheless fully cooperated with the Department’s investigation and timely and appropriately remediated the misconduct. As a result, its disclosure qualified as a “Near Miss” Voluntary Self-Disclosure under the Policy.

“This non-prosecution agreement and million-dollar criminal penalty mark the successful resolution of our investigation into the illegal sale of advanced networking equipment and services to a Russian weapons manufacturer, in clear violation of U.S. sanctions and export controls,” said Assistant Director Roman Rozhavsky of the FBI’s Counterintelligence and Espionage Division. “The FBI remains dedicated to keeping sensitive technology out of the hands of the Russian military, and we're grateful to Homeland Security Investigations and the Bureau of Industry and Security for their partnership on this case. Let this announcement serve as a clear warning: if you attempt to arm our adversaries by violating U.S. law, justice will find you.”

“HSI remains committed to investigating companies and individuals who evade U.S. export controls and sanctions to provide goods or services to foreign weapons manufacturers,” said Acting Special Agent in Charge Jeremy Pierczynski of Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) Detroit. “These laws protect our national security and prevent U.S.-origin products and services from supporting adversaries’ military capabilities. HSI will continue working with our law enforcement and regulatory partners to identify and hold accountable those who undermine these critical safeguards.”

The agreement arose out of an investigation into Extreme Networks’ sales of products and services to Moscow Machinery Building Plant Avangard (MMZA), a Russian weapons manufacturer that was owned by JSC Concern Almaz-Antey (Almaz Antey), which was added to the Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons List by the Department of the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in July 2014.

Pursuant to the non-prosecution agreement, Extreme Networks will forfeit $487,860.92 in proceeds from the sanctions and export control offenses and pay a criminal fine of $487,860.92, for a total criminal penalty of $975,721.84. Extreme Networks will also resolve a parallel administrative action by OFAC.

Between around March 2018 and March 2022, Extreme Networks, through its then-Russia based subsidiary, Extreme Networks Rus LLC, processed and fulfilled 11 purchase orders for networking equipment and services to MMZA without the required license or authorization from OFAC. MMZA was a primary producer of the S-300 and S-400 anti-aircraft missile systems used by the Russian army. To facilitate these sales, certain Russia-based Extreme Networks employees concealed the identity of MMZA from Extreme Networks’ global trade compliance group, causing Extreme Networks to file false electronic export information via the Automated Export System and smuggle goods from the United States. Through this scheme, Extreme Networks deprived the U.S. government of its ability to carry out its lawful function of enforcing sanctions and export controls designed to protect national security and economic interests. As a result of its unlawful conduct, Extreme Networks earned approximately $487,860.92 in revenue from the sales of goods and services.

Although Extreme Networks’ self-disclosure to NSD was not timely pursuant to the Policy, Extreme Networks nonetheless cooperated with the Department’s investigation by timely providing relevant facts and documents and making employees available for interviews. Extreme Networks also appropriately remediated the misconduct by terminating its contract with the third-party distributor it used to facilitate these sales, improving screening procedures, hiring additional compliance personnel, and implementing diligence procedures in connection with mergers and acquisitions. Given these steps and the lack of aggravating circumstances, the Department agreed to enter into a non-prosecution agreement.

The FBI Charlotte Field Office, the Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security, and Homeland Security Investigations investigated the case.

This case was prosecuted by former Trial Attorney Maria Fedor of the National Security Division’s Counterintelligence and Export Control Section and Assistant U.S. Attorney Adam Hulbig for the Eastern District of North Carolina.

Please see the Justice Department’s policy here.

#7834. Is It Safe to Use a Fireplace I Haven’t Cleaned in Years?

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

Published Nov 15, 2026 10:00 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

A fireplace should be a source of warmth, comfort, and connection in your home, not a source of worry, says Chris Maxson, owner and CEO of Acucraft Fireplaces in Big Lake, Minnesota. But it takes some effort and upkeep to ensure your family and home stay safe. If your fireplace hasn’t been cleaned or professionally inspected in years, don’t light a fire until you’ve had it evaluated.

“Just because a fireplace looks fine on the outside doesn’t mean it’s safe to operate,” warns Maxson. Even when a fireplace sits unused, the chimney can develop obstructions from animal nests, leaves, and other debris. In addition, moisture intrusion, deterioration, and damaged components can create potential safety concerns. Whether you have a traditional wood-burning fireplace or a modern gas fireplace, you’ll want to understand how best to clean and maintain it.

It’s not safe to use a fireplace that has been neglected for an extended period. In general, you should clean a wood-burning fireplace and the chimney once a year before you start using it. Likewise, gas fireplaces need cleaning once a year or as recommended by the manufacturer. Here are the reasons to clean fireplaces, according to Maxson:

Wood-burning fireplaces produce soot, ash, and creosote as wood burns. Creosote is highly combustible, and accumulated deposits can increase the risk of a chimney fire. Both gas and wood-burning fireplaces also rely on properly functioning venting systems to direct combustion byproducts away from occupied spaces. Obstructions or damaged venting can contribute to dangerous conditions, including carbon monoxide exposure inside homes.

A clean, properly maintained fireplace is more likely to operate as designed. On the other hand, excessive buildup, restricted airflow, and neglected components can interfere with ignition, combustion, and draft.

Cleaning a fireplace isn’t just about making it look good. It’s about making sure the entire system—including the components you can’t see—is functioning properly. Preventive maintenance protects both your home and your investment.

Maxson recommends that homeowners have their fireplace professionally inspected at least once a year, even if they don’t use it very often. “Cleaning removes buildup, while an inspection helps identify hidden issues that cleaning alone won’t solve,” he explains.

For wood-burning fireplaces, annual chimney inspections are essential. “A qualified chimney professional can determine whether sweeping is necessary based on creosote accumulation, soot, debris, and other conditions,” explains Maxson. “Homeowners who burn wood frequently may require additional cleaning during the heating season” for their fireplaces. The firebox also requires routine attention; ash. Remove ash as needed, based on the manufacturer’s instructions, and keep the surrounding area free of combustible debris.

Gas fireplaces should also receive regular professional maintenance according to the manufacturer’s recommendations, typically including an annual inspection. “Servicing may involve cleaning the burner and other components, inspecting the ignition system, and verifying proper operation and venting,” explains Maxson.

Wood-burning fireplaces should routinely be cleaned to manage ash and creosote buildup. A professional chimney sweep can remove accumulated deposits and evaluate the chimney for obstructions, deterioration, or damage. While gas fireplaces burn cleaner than wood-burning fireplaces in terms of ash and creosote production, that doesn’t mean they’re maintenance free, says Maxson. “Gas fireplaces can accumulate dust, debris, and residue,” he explains. “One of the biggest mistakes gas fireplace owners make is assuming that because there’s no wood or ash to clean up, there’s nothing to maintain.”

Equipped with a fire-resistant filter that captures fine ash particles, this vacuum earned the top spot in our tested buyer’s guide.

The real danger is that many fireplace problems aren’t visible until something goes wrong, says Maxson. “A chimney obstruction, damaged venting component, or buildup of creosote can exist without any obvious warning signs, and that’s why regular inspections and cleaning are so important.” Maxson warns about the following problems that can occur:

Here are some additional tips to keep in mind, according to Maxson:

Every home with a fuel-burning fireplace should have working smoke and carbon monoxide alarms installed in appropriate locations. Test them regularly and follow manufacturer recommendations for replacement.

For wood-burning fireplaces, use properly seasoned, dry firewood. Avoid burning treated lumber, painted wood, household trash, or other materials that can release harmful chemicals or contribute to excessive deposits.

Furniture, rugs, blankets, decorations, and firewood should remain outside the manufacturer’s required clearance areas.

Wood-burning fireplaces can release sparks and embers, while fireplace glass and exposed surfaces can become extremely hot. Proper screens and barriers help reduce the risk of burns and accidental contact.

Ashes and embers can remain hot long after a fire appears to be extinguished. Allow them to cool, place them in a covered metal container, and store that container outdoors on a noncombustible surface away from structures and other combustible materials.

Unusual odors, smoke entering the home, difficulty igniting a gas fireplace, abnormal flame patterns, visible damage, or unexplained soot accumulation are all reasons to stop using the fireplace and have it evaluated. If you smell gas, leave the area immediately and contact your gas utility or emergency services from a safe location.

#7833. At Large Circuit Nominees?

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

If the blue slip is abolished for district courts, it should be obliterated for circuit courts.

During the first Trump Administration, the blue slip policy was effectively eliminated for circuit court judges. The goal, of course, was to ensure that states with one or more Democratic senators would not be able to block all circuit court nominees. Still, the blue slip policy remained for district court judges through Trump 1.0, the Biden Administration, and Trump 2.0. Does anyone expect the blue slip policy for district court judges to survive if a Democrat wins the White House in 2028 with 56+ Senators? I am doubtful. Indeed, given how Democrats blocked so many U.S. Attorney nominees, I am doubtful the blue slip endures even for that position.

Let's just assume the blue slip policy is eliminated for district court judges. Should the Republicans ever regain power, I propose a thought experiment: actually eliminate the blue slip for circuit judges. As I've noted, circuit court judges belong to the circuit, not the state. It is a mistake to even think of a "home state senator" for a circuit court seat. Of course seats are affiliated with a state by virtue of custom, but nothing in the statute requires it. If Congress wants to assign a seat to a state, they can easily do so. But a Circuit Court Judge decides cases that affect all of the states in a circuit. Indeed, over time, some seats have "switched" between states.

The President could perhaps facilitate that process by making all circuit court nominees "at large." In other words, the President could solicit nominees from candidates in all states in that circuit. If a Fifth Circuit seat opens up, the Senators from Texas, Louisiana, and Mississippi could all make recommendations, and the President could pick the best candidate all around. Likewise, if an Eighth Circuit seat opens up, the Senators from the states between North Dakota and Arkansas can make recommendations.

First, and foremost, requiring this much consultation can gum up the process. Dealing with one set of senators is a lot of work. Multiplying that by many more can become impossible. But it would be just that--a consultation. The White House would only have to interview the judges that clear the bar. Again, no actual blue slip. I suspect if you rank all of the nominees circuit-wide, few would make the cut.

Second, some senators are very good at picking judges. Opening up the process to so many not-so-good senators, can make the process worse. Indeed, Senators are democratically accountable, while people in OLP and the White House Counsel's Office are largely unknown. I think the response is that very few few Senators are actually good at this process. My goodness, the Senators from Mississippi and Arkansas should be permanently disqualified from picking their friends as judges. I think my recommendation would, on balance, get far more strong judges than the status quo. Of course, the President can give more deference to senators with proven track records of picking judges.

Third, Senators are unlikely to go along with this process, and will not give up their customary prerogative. Again, in my hypothetical, the blue slip is gone for district court judges, so it will be a different world. Indeed, given that district court judges can issue universal vacaturs that affect the entire country, I'm not sure why senators should have that much control. The Senate can of course vote down a nominee, but that would have to be a vote they are accountable for. Would Senators Boozman and Cotton have voted down Judge Rudofsky on the floor? Probably not.

This is just a thought experiment. Fodder to consider for the future. That is, unless the Grand Old Party goes the way of the Federalists and the Whigs.

Josh Blackman is a constitutional law professor at the South Texas College of Law Houston and the President of the Harlan Institute. Follow him @JoshMBlackman.

#7832. American Woman Convicted of Receiving Military Training from ISIS in Syria

An official website of the United States government
